options.text: neccessary
options.why: Necessary has one c, not two.

options.text: necesary
options.why: Necessary has a double s.

options.text: necessary
nessesary
options.why: Necessary has a c after the first e.

hints: This word has one double letter.
Remember: one collar and two sleeves. That means one c and two s.
Write n-e-c, then think about the double letter.
items.explanation: Necessary has one c and two s, like a shirt with one collar and two sleeves.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses its or it’s correctly?

options.text: The dog wagged it’s tail.
options.why: It’s means it is. The dog wagged it is tail does not make sense.

options.text: The dog wagged its tail.
The dog wagged its’ tail.
options.why: Its’ is not a word.

options.text: The dogs wagged it’s tails.
options.why: It’s means it is, and the dogs are plural.

hints: Its shows belonging. It’s is short for it is.
Test each sentence by replacing the word with it is.
Does the tail belong to the dog?
items.explanation: Its shows that the tail belongs to the dog. It’s always means it is or it has.

items.prompt: One word is spelt wrongly. Write it correctly. We definately need more chairs.
hints: Find the word that looks unusual.
This word contains the smaller word finite.
Find the smaller word inside first, then add the beginning and the ending.
items.explanation: Definitely contains the word finite: de-finite-ly.

items.prompt: Sort these into complete sentences and sentence fragments.
hints: A complete sentence makes sense on its own.
A fragment is missing a subject, a verb or a main clause.
Read each one aloud. Does it leave you waiting for more?
items.explanation: Because the bus was late and Although it rained are subordinate clauses with no main clause. Running along the beach has no subject.

options.text: There are less pupils in the library today.
options.why: Use fewer with things you can count, such as pupils.

options.text: There are fewer pupils in the library today.
There are lesser pupils in the library today.
options.why: Lesser means not as important, not a smaller number.

options.text: There is fewer pupils in the library today.
options.why: Pupils is plural, so the verb should be are.

hints: Pupils are things you can count.
Use fewer with things you can count and less with things you cannot count, such as water.
Check the verb too: is or are?
items.explanation: Pupils can be counted, so we use fewer. Pupils is plural, so the verb is are.

options.text: Each of the pupils have a locker.
options.why: The subject is each, which is singular.

options.text: Each of the pupil has a locker.
options.why: After each of, the noun should be plural: pupils.

options.text: Each of the pupils having a locker.
options.why: This has no main verb.

options.text: Each of the pupils has a locker.

hints: Find the real subject of the sentence.
The subject is each, which means every single one.
Is each singular or plural? Choose the verb to match.
items.explanation: Each is singular, so it takes has: Each of the pupils has a locker.

items.prompt: Two words are the wrong homophones. Write the correct words in order. The teacher praised the hole class for there teamwork. ___ ___
hints: Look for words that sound right but are spelt for a different meaning.
One word should mean all of something. The other should show belonging.
Start with hole. Is the teacher talking about a gap in the ground?
items.explanation: Whole means all of the class, and their shows the teamwork belongs to the class.

items.prompt: Read: Last week our class visit the botanic gardens in Bogor. We seen hundreds of orchids and a giant flower. Everyone enjoyed the trip. Choose all the mistakes.

options.text: Visit should be visited.
Seen should be saw.
Bogor should not have a capital letter.
options.why: Bogor is the name of a city, so it needs a capital letter.

options.text: Enjoyed should be enjoy.
options.why: The trip is in the past, so enjoyed is correct.

options.text: Everyone should be Everybody’s.
options.why: Everyone is correct here as the subject.

hints: Last week tells you the text is in the past tense.
Check each verb: is it in the simple past tense?
Find the verbs visit, seen and enjoyed. Which ones need changing?
items.explanation: The text is about last week, so visit should be visited. Seen needs a helping verb, so the simple past saw is correct here.

items.prompt: Which is the best edit to remove repetition? The beach was beautiful. The sand was beautiful and the sea was beautiful too.

options.text: The beach was beautiful: the sand was golden and the sea was a clear turquoise.
The beach was beautiful. The sand was beautiful. The sea was beautiful.
options.why: This still repeats beautiful three times.

options.text: The beach was nice. The sand was nice and the sea was nice too.
options.why: This swaps one repeated word for another.

options.text: The beach, the sand, the sea.
options.why: This is not a complete sentence.

hints: The word beautiful appears three times.
Good editing replaces repeated words with precise details.
Look for the option that describes the sand and the sea in different ways.
items.explanation: The best edit keeps beautiful once and adds precise details, golden and clear turquoise, instead of repeating it.

items.prompt: Which sentence is correct and clear?

options.text: While walking to school, a rainbow appeared in the sky.
options.why: This sounds as if the rainbow was walking to school.

options.text: While I was walking to school, I saw a rainbow.
Walking to school, the rainbow was bright.
options.why: This sounds as if the rainbow was walking.

options.text: While walking to school, a rainbow saw me.
options.why: Rainbows cannot see, and this sounds as if the rainbow was walking.

hints: Look at who is doing the walking in each sentence.
The opening phrase must describe the subject that comes straight after the comma.
Ask in each sentence: who or what was walking to school?
items.explanation: In the correct sentence, it is clear that I was walking and I saw the rainbow. In the others, the opening phrase seems to describe the rainbow.
